title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
definition: The World Health Organization checklist has three pauses: before anesthesia, before incision, and before leaving the OR. The team confirms identity, site, antibiotics, and counts aloud. Hospitals using it cut surgical deaths measurably.
patient_flow: Patients check in, change, and wait in pre-op holding where the surgeon marks the site and anesthesia reviews the plan. In the OR, the team does a time-out — confirming patient, site, and procedure aloud — then operates. Afterward the patient wakes in PACU under close monitoring until discharge criteria are met, then goes to a floor, home, or ICU.
teaching: Simple: the core idea in plain words — what it is and why it matters.

title: The Time-Out Ritual
definition: Right before the first cut, everything stops: the surgeon states the patient's name, the procedure, and the site, and the team agrees. This single pause prevents wrong-site surgery. It is required by accreditation everywhere.

title: Sponge and Instrument Counts
definition: Scrub nurses count every sponge, needle, and instrument before the case and again before closure. Counts must match exactly — a missing sponge means an X-ray before the patient leaves the room. Retained objects are a 'never event.'

title: General Anesthesia
definition: General anesthesia renders the patient unconscious, pain-free, and still using IV drugs and inhaled gases. The anesthesiologist manages the airway, breathing, and blood pressure throughout. Waking happens in PACU as the drugs wear off.

title: Regional Anesthesia
definition: Spinals, epidurals, and nerve blocks numb only the surgical region while the patient stays awake or lightly sedated. Recovery is faster with less nausea and less opioid need. Hips, knees, and C-sections commonly use regional techniques.

title: Sterile Field Technique
definition: Everything touching the surgical site must be sterile: gowns, gloves, drapes, and instruments. The scrub nurse guards the field, and anything contaminated is removed immediately. One break in sterility can seed a deep infection.

title: Electrosurgery
definition: Electrosurgical units cut tissue and seal blood vessels with electric current, reducing bleeding dramatically. The surgeon switches between cut and coagulation modes with a foot pedal. A grounding pad protects the patient from burns.

title: Minimally Invasive Laparoscopy
definition: Laparoscopy operates through small incisions using a camera and long instruments, instead of one large open cut. Patients have less pain, smaller scars, and faster discharge. Gallbladders, hernias, and many gynecologic cases are done this way.

title: Robotic-Assisted Surgery
definition: The surgeon sits at a console driving robotic arms with wristed instruments that bend beyond human range. A 3D magnified view shows tiny structures clearly. Prostate, colorectal, and gynecologic surgery commonly use robots.

title: Pre-Op Holding
definition: In pre-op, nurses verify identity, allergies, and fasting, start IVs, and give pre-op antibiotics. The surgeon marks the operative site with initials. Anesthesia does a final airway and history review before wheeling to the OR.

title: PACU Recovery
definition: The post-anesthesia care unit watches patients wake up: breathing, blood pressure, pain, nausea, and bleeding. Nurses use the Aldrete score to judge readiness for discharge. Most patients spend one to two hours here.

title: Aldrete Discharge Score
definition: The Aldrete score rates activity, breathing, circulation, consciousness, and oxygen — 0 to 2 points each. A score of 9 or 10 means safe discharge from PACU. It turns 'ready to go' into an objective number.

title: Surgical Site Infection Prevention
definition: Infection prevention starts before the incision: antibiotics within 60 minutes, clipping (not shaving) hair, skin prep with chlorhexidine, and sterile technique. Post-op, wounds are watched for redness, drainage, and fever.

title: Patient Positioning
definition: Patients are positioned — supine, prone, lateral, lithotomy — to expose the surgical site while protecting nerves and pressure points. Padding guards elbows, heels, and eyes. Poor positioning can injure nerves that take months to heal.

title: Specimen Handling
definition: Tissue removed in surgery goes to pathology in labeled containers, sometimes rushed as a 'frozen section' for a diagnosis while the patient is still asleep. Correct labeling ties every specimen to the right patient and site — a mix-up is catastrophic.

title: OR Turnover
definition: Between cases, the room is cleaned, trash removed, surfaces disinfected, and fresh sterile setups brought in. Fast, thorough turnover keeps the schedule moving without cutting corners. Average turnover runs 20 to 30 minutes.

title: Block Scheduling
definition: OR time is scheduled in blocks assigned to surgical services — orthopedics gets two rooms on Mondays, for example. Unused block time is released to others. Good scheduling fills rooms without running past midnight.

title: Emergency Surgery Readiness
definition: One OR stays ready around the clock for ruptured appendixes, trauma, and emergency C-sections. The on-call team can have the room open within 30 minutes. Elective schedules flex around true emergencies.

title: Implant Tracking
definition: Every implant — hips, knees, pacemakers, mesh — is logged with lot and serial numbers tied to the patient. If a manufacturer recalls a device, the hospital can find every affected patient in minutes. This registry is a patient-safety backbone.

title: Wound Closure Techniques
definition: Surgeons close wounds in layers: deep sutures for strength, skin sutures or staples for the surface, sometimes glue for small cuts. The method balances strength, healing, and scarring. Drains may be left to prevent fluid buildup.
